diseases.name: Early Blight
diseases.description: Early blight is a common fungal disease of tomatoes caused by Alternaria solani. It primarily affects older leaves but can also impact stems and fruit. The disease is characterized by dark, concentric-ringed lesions.
symptoms: Dark brown to black lesions with concentric rings (target-like pattern) on lower/older leaves
Yellowing of tissue around lesions
Progressive defoliation starting from the bottom of the plant
Dark, sunken lesions on stems near the soil line
Leathery, dark spots on fruit near the stem end
causes: Fungal pathogen Alternaria solani surviving in infected plant debris
Warm temperatures (24–29°C) combined with high humidity or frequent rainfall
Poor air circulation due to dense planting
immediate_actions: Remove and destroy infected leaves to reduce spore load
Improve air circulation by pruning lower branches
Avoid overhead watering; use drip irrigation instead
Apply locally approved fungicide if disease is progressing. Use only locally approved agricultural products according to label instructions and local agricultural guidance.
Stake or cage plants to keep foliage off the ground
preventive_actions: Use disease-resistant tomato varieties when available
Practice crop rotation (2-3 year cycle, avoid other Solanaceae)
Mulch around plants to prevent soil splash onto lower leaves
Maintain proper plant spacing for good air circulation
Remove all crop debris after harvest
Ensure adequate nutrition, especially potassium and calcium
monitoring_advice: Inspect lower/older leaves weekly for early lesion development
Monitor weather for warm, humid conditions that favor the disease
Check after rainfall or overhead irrigation events
Track disease progression — if lesions spread to upper canopy, escalate treatment

environmental_conditions.rainfall: Frequent rainfall or overhead irrigation increases risk

diseases.expert_escalation: Consult an agricultural extension officer if lesions cover more than 30% of foliage, if the disease is spreading rapidly despite management, or if you are unsure about appropriate treatment options.

diseases.name: Late Blight
diseases.description: Late blight is a devastating disease that can rapidly destroy entire tomato crops. It caused the Irish Potato Famine and remains one of the most destructive plant diseases worldwide.
symptoms: Large, irregularly shaped, water-soaked lesions on leaves
White, fuzzy mold growth on the underside of leaves in humid conditions
Dark brown to black lesions that spread rapidly across the canopy
Firm, dark brown blotches on fruit
Rapid wilting and death of entire plants within days
causes: Cool temperatures (15–22°C) with high humidity or prolonged leaf wetness
Infected seed potatoes or volunteer potato plants nearby
immediate_actions: Remove and destroy all infected plants immediately — do NOT compost
Apply locally approved fungicide immediately to remaining healthy plants. Use only locally approved agricultural products according to label instructions and local agricultural guidance.
Increase monitoring frequency to daily
Notify neighboring farmers — late blight spreads very rapidly through airborne spores
preventive_actions: Avoid planting tomatoes near potato fields
Ensure good air circulation and wide spacing
Use drip irrigation, never overhead watering
Remove all volunteer potato/tomato plants in the area
Apply preventive fungicides during high-risk weather periods
monitoring_advice: Monitor daily during cool, wet weather periods
Check lower canopy and stems first
Look for white sporulation on leaf undersides early in the morning
Use late blight forecasting tools if available in your region

environmental_conditions.rainfall: Cool, rainy weather dramatically increases risk

diseases.expert_escalation: Seek immediate professional help at first sign of late blight. This disease can destroy an entire crop within 7–10 days under favorable conditions.

diseases.name: Leaf Mold
diseases.description: Leaf mold is primarily a greenhouse and high-tunnel disease of tomatoes. It thrives in high-humidity environments with poor air circulation.
symptoms: Light green to yellowish spots on upper leaf surfaces
Olive-green to brown velvety mold growth on lower leaf surfaces
Leaves may curl, wither, and drop
Usually starts on older, lower leaves and progresses upward
causes: Fungal pathogen Passalora fulva (previously Cladosporium fulvum)
Poor ventilation in greenhouses or high tunnels
Dense plant canopy restricting air flow
immediate_actions: Improve ventilation immediately — open greenhouse vents or remove side walls
Remove heavily infected lower leaves
Reduce humidity through proper watering practices
Avoid wetting foliage during irrigation
monitoring_advice: Regularly check lower leaf undersides for early mold growth
Monitor greenhouse humidity levels — keep below 85% when possible
Increase monitoring during warm, humid periods

environmental_conditions.rainfall: More common in enclosed growing environments

diseases.expert_escalation: Consult if mold is spreading despite improved ventilation, or if you need guidance on resistant varieties for your region.

diseases.name: Septoria Leaf Spot
diseases.description: Septoria leaf spot is one of the most common and destructive foliar diseases of tomatoes. It causes numerous small, circular spots that can rapidly defoliate plants.
symptoms: Numerous small (2–3mm), circular spots with dark borders and gray-tan centers
Tiny black dots (pycnidia) visible in the center of lesions under magnification
Extensive yellowing and leaf drop
Usually starts on lower leaves and progresses upward
Rarely affects fruit directly but reduces yield through defoliation
causes: Splash from rain or irrigation spreading spores
Pathogen survives in infected crop debris
immediate_actions: Remove infected lower leaves
Apply mulch to prevent soil splash
Switch to drip irrigation if using overhead watering
Apply locally approved fungicide if spread is rapid. Use only locally approved agricultural products according to label instructions and local agricultural guidance.
preventive_actions: Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
Stake and prune plants for air circulation
Remove all plant debris at season end
monitoring_advice: Check lower leaves weekly during the growing season
Look for tiny circular spots with gray centers
Monitor especially after wet weather events

environmental_conditions.rainfall: Rain splash is primary dispersal mechanism

diseases.expert_escalation: Consult if defoliation exceeds 40% or if you need help selecting appropriate fungicide programs.

diseases.name: Bacterial Spot
diseases.description: Bacterial spot is a serious disease of tomatoes and peppers caused by several species of Xanthomonas bacteria. It affects leaves, stems, and fruit.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves
Spots become angular and may have a yellow halo
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow and drop
Raised, scab-like lesions on fruit
Spots on stems appear as elongated dark streaks
causes: Splash dispersal from rain or irrigation
Bacteria enter through natural openings or wounds
immediate_actions: Avoid working with plants when foliage is wet
Remove severely infected plants
Apply copper-based bactericide if locally approved. Use only locally approved agricultural products according to label instructions and local agricultural guidance.
Reduce overhead irrigation
preventive_actions: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants
monitoring_advice: Inspect transplants before planting
Monitor after storms or heavy rain
Check fruit for scab-like lesions as they develop

environmental_conditions.humidity: Warm, humid conditions with rain promote spread
environmental_conditions.rainfall: Rain splash is the primary means of spread

diseases.expert_escalation: Consult if bacterial spot is confirmed and spreading rapidly, especially in commercial production. There are no curative treatments for bacterial diseases.

diseases.name: Target Spot
diseases.description: Target spot is caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola and can affect leaves, stems, and fruit of tomato plants.
symptoms: Small, dark brown spots that enlarge to form target-like concentric rings
Lesions may have a yellow halo
Spots on fruit are sunken with concentric rings
Lower and middle leaves are affected first
immediate_actions: Remove infected leaves
Improve air circulation by pruning
Apply locally approved fungicide. Use only locally approved agricultural products according to label instructions and local agricultural guidance.
monitoring_advice: Regular foliar inspection
Monitor during warm, humid weather
diseases.expert_escalation: Consult if disease persists despite management.

diseases.name: Tomato Mosaic Virus
diseases.description: Tomato mosaic virus causes mottling and distortion of leaves. It is highly stable and can persist on tools, clothing, and in soil.
symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic mottling on leaves
Leaf curling and distortion
Reduced fruit set and yield
Yellow-green mottling on fruit
Stunted plant growth
causes: Mechanical transmission through handling and tools
Very stable virus — persists on surfaces for long periods
immediate_actions: Do NOT handle healthy plants after touching infected ones
Remove and destroy infected plants
Wash hands with soap and water before handling other plants
Disinfect all tools with a solution of milk or trisodium phosphate
preventive_actions: Use TMV/ToMV-resistant varieties (most modern varieties have Tm-2 resistance)
Do not use tobacco products near tomato plants
monitoring_advice: Look for mosaic patterns on young leaves
Check for leaf distortion and curling
Monitor transplant sources

environmental_conditions.optimal_temperature: Virus is active across a wide temperature range
environmental_conditions.rainfall: Spread is primarily mechanical, not weather-driven

diseases.expert_escalation: Consult to confirm virus identity through lab testing if mosaic symptoms are observed.

diseases.name: Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
diseases.description: TYLCV is a devastating begomovirus transmitted by whiteflies. It causes severe stunting and yield loss in tomatoes.
symptoms: Severe upward curling of leaflet margins
Pronounced yellowing of leaves
Stunted, bushy plant growth
Flower drop and drastically reduced fruit set
Plants infected early may produce no fruit
causes: Begomovirus transmitted by silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
immediate_actions: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Implement whitefly management (sticky traps, reflective mulch)
Control whiteflies on remaining plants. Use only locally approved agricultural products according to label instructions and local agricultural guidance.
Remove weed hosts around the field
preventive_actions: Implement a whitefly-free period before planting
Use reflective mulch to repel whiteflies
monitoring_advice: Monitor whitefly populations with yellow sticky traps
Check young plants for curling and yellowing symptoms
Scout field borders for whitefly-infested weeds

environmental_conditions.humidity: Moderate to low humidity favors whiteflies
environmental_conditions.rainfall: Dry, warm conditions increase whitefly populations

diseases.expert_escalation: Consult immediately if TYLCV is suspected — early removal and whitefly management are critical to prevent field-wide spread.

diseases.name: Spider Mites (Two-spotted)
diseases.description: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny arachnid pests that feed on leaf cells, causing stippling, yellowing, and eventual defoliation.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling on upper leaf surfaces
Fine webbing on leaf undersides and between leaves
Leaves turn bronze, dry out, and drop
Tiny moving dots visible on leaf undersides (mites are <0.5mm)
Severe infestations cause plant stress and yield loss
causes: Hot, dry conditions favor rapid population buildup
Overuse of broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators
immediate_actions: Spray plant undersides with a strong jet of water to dislodge mites
Apply miticide or insecticidal soap. Use only locally approved agricultural products according to label instructions and local agricultural guidance.
Increase irrigation to reduce plant stress
Consider releasing predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis)
preventive_actions: Control dust in and around fields
Monitor regularly in hot, dry weather
monitoring_advice: Check leaf undersides weekly with a hand lens
Look for stippling on upper leaf surfaces as an early sign
Tap leaves over white paper to see dislodged mites
Monitor during hot, dry weather when populations spike

environmental_conditions.humidity: Low humidity favors mite reproduction (inverse of most diseases)
environmental_conditions.rainfall: Heavy rain can knock mites off plants

diseases.expert_escalation: Consult for biological control options or resistance management if chemical treatments are losing effectiveness.

diseases.name: Healthy
diseases.description: The tomato plant appears healthy with no visible signs of disease or pest damage.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
immediate_actions: No immediate action required
Continue standard crop maintenance
preventive_actions: Ensure adequate nutrition through balanced fertilization
Practice crop rotation in future seasons
Monitor regularly for early detection of any issues
monitoring_advice: Continue weekly visual inspections
Monitor weather conditions for disease-favorable periods
Keep records of plant health for future reference
diseases.expert_escalation: Routine consultation for general crop management advice if desired.

diseases.name: Early Blight
diseases.description: Early blight of potato is caused by the same pathogen as tomato early blight. It causes concentric-ringed lesions and can significantly reduce tuber yield.
symptoms: Dark brown lesions with concentric rings on lower leaves
Lesions may coalesce, causing extensive leaf death
Premature defoliation reduces tuber size
Tuber lesions appear as dark, sunken spots
causes: Warm temperatures and alternating wet/dry conditions
immediate_actions: Remove infected leaves if practical
Apply locally approved fungicide. Use only locally approved agricultural products according to label instructions and local agricultural guidance.
Ensure adequate irrigation to reduce plant stress
preventive_actions: Maintain adequate fertility (especially nitrogen and potassium)
monitoring_advice: Begin scouting when plants are 15cm tall
Monitor lower canopy weekly
Intensify monitoring after warm, wet weather

environmental_conditions.humidity: Alternating wet and dry promotes sporulation

diseases.expert_escalation: Consult for integrated pest management programs in commercial potato production.

diseases.name: Late Blight
diseases.description: Late blight of potato is the same disease that caused the Irish Potato Famine. It can destroy a potato crop within days under favorable conditions.
symptoms: Water-soaked, dark lesions on leaves, often starting at tips or edges
White mold growth on leaf undersides
Rapid browning and death of foliage
Firm, reddish-brown granular rot in tubers
Entire fields can be devastated within a week
causes: Cool (10–20°C), wet conditions with high humidity
Airborne sporangia can travel long distances
immediate_actions: Apply fungicide immediately to healthy plants. Use only locally approved agricultural products according to label instructions and local agricultural guidance.
Destroy all infected plant material — do NOT compost
Inform neighboring growers
Do not harvest tubers until 2–3 weeks after vine death to prevent tuber infection
preventive_actions: Use late blight forecasting models (BLITECAST) if available
Apply preventive fungicides during high-risk periods
Destroy volunteer potatoes and cull piles
monitoring_advice: Daily monitoring during cool, wet weather
Check field borders and low-lying areas first
Use regional late blight tracking systems if available

environmental_conditions.rainfall: Cool, rainy weather is the primary driver

diseases.expert_escalation: Seek immediate professional assistance at first suspicion of late blight. Delay can result in total crop loss.

diseases.name: Healthy
diseases.description: The potato plant appears healthy with no visible signs of disease.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
immediate_actions: No immediate action required
Continue standard crop care
preventive_actions: Hill potatoes regularly to prevent tuber greening
monitoring_advice: Continue regular visual inspections
Monitor for Colorado potato beetle and other pests
Watch for late blight alerts in your region
diseases.expert_escalation: Routine consultation for fertility and pest management if desired.

diseases.name: Bacterial Spot
diseases.description: Bacterial spot of pepper is caused by Xanthomonas species and is one of the most serious diseases of pepper worldwide.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves
Spots become raised, scab-like on fruit
Severe defoliation in wet conditions
Fruit spots reduce marketability
immediate_actions: Avoid handling plants when wet
Remove severely infected plants
Apply copper-based bactericide if locally approved. Use only locally approved agricultural products according to label instructions and local agricultural guidance.
Switch to drip irrigation
preventive_actions: Practice crop rotation (2+ years with non-solanaceous crops)
monitoring_advice: Inspect transplants before planting
Monitor after rain events
Check for leaf spots and fruit scab

environmental_conditions.humidity: High humidity with rain promotes spread
environmental_conditions.rainfall: Rain splash is the primary dispersal mechanism

diseases.expert_escalation: Consult for resistance management and integrated disease management programs.

diseases.name: Healthy
diseases.description: The pepper plant appears healthy with no visible signs of disease.
symptoms: No disease symptoms detected
immediate_actions: No immediate action required
Continue standard care
preventive_actions: Monitor for pests such as aphids and pepper weevils
monitoring_advice: Weekly visual inspections
Monitor for insect pests
Watch for signs of nutrient deficiency
